title: How to Survive a Plane Crash
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss surviving a plane crash. Josh shares his fear of flying, including a rough Miami-to-Atlanta flight, and they cite odds: about one in eleven million for being involved in an airline crash versus one in five thousand for a car crash. They explain why negative media coverage skews perception and the lack of control factor. They note that many people survive crashes, with more than half of extreme crashes between 1980 and 2000 having survivors. Popular Mechanics data suggests rear-seat passengers are more likely to survive. Tips include counting rows to the exit, the revised brace position (arms extended, hands crossed against the seat back, head resting on hands), dressing in long sleeves and closed-toe shoes, dividing family responsibilities, listening to pre-flight instructions, and putting on your own oxygen mask first. They recount the 1972 Andes crash of the Uruguayan rugby team and the movie Alive. They advise getting low to avoid smoke and fumes, moving far from the plane after exiting, leaving baggage and pets behind, not inflating life vests inside the cabin, and staying calm. They close with a Dominion University study finding crash survivors reported better emotional outlook, and a plug for a HowStuffWorks article by Molly Edmonds.

segments.title: Opening banter and fear of flying
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, discussing the worst ways to die and Josh's fear of flying, including a stressful flight from Miami to Atlanta.

segments.title: Odds of dying in a plane crash
segments.summary: They compare the odds of being in an airline crash (about one in eleven million) with car crashes (one in five thousand), attributing the perception gap to lack of control and negative news coverage. A statistic about flying every day for thirty-five thousand years is cited from air-disaster.com.
topics: car crash vs plane crash risk

segments.title: Survival rates in crashes
segments.summary: They note that many crashes have survivors, with more than half of extreme crashes from 1980 to 2000 having survivors, and that most crashes are take-off or landing accidents.

segments.title: Safest seat on the plane
segments.summary: The FAA does not name a safest seat. Popular Mechanics data over thirty-six years found passengers in the rear of the plane more likely to survive than those in the front.

segments.title: Preparing before and after boarding
segments.summary: Tips include counting rows to the nearest exit, the updated brace position with arms extended, hands crossed on the seat back and head resting on hands, dressing in long sleeves and closed-toe shoes, dividing child responsibility between parents, and listening to pre-flight instructions.

segments.title: Andes crash and the Uruguayan rugby team
segments.summary: They recount the crash of a plane carrying the Uruguayan rugby team and others in the Andes, with survivors resorting to cannibalism over seventy-two days, and the movie Alive based on it.

segments.title: Evacuation and what to do after leaving the plane
segments.summary: They discuss the golden ninety seconds for evacuation, getting low to avoid smoke and fumes, moving far from the plane, leaving baggage and pets behind, not inflating life vests inside the cabin, and the oxygen mask rule.

segments.title: Emotional outlook of crash survivors
segments.summary: A Dominion University study of fifteen survivors found they reported a more positive outlook and fewer stress signs than a control group, with the highest scores among those who felt in control or helped others off the plane. Staying calm is stressed as key.

segments.title: Sign-off and article plug
segments.summary: The hosts plug Molly Edmonds' article on whether people get wiser with age and point listeners to the site's survival articles, then close the show.
